parole.testo: From French -ette (feminine of -et (diminutive suffix)), from Latin -itta. In some words, from these related sources: * English -ette (from the same French etymon) * the French masculine -et * Italian -etto (from the same Latin etymon) Doublet of -ita and -eta.

parole.significato: absinthe; wormwood (Artemisia absinthium, a herb of Eurasia and northern Africa)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French absinthe, from Latin absinthium.

From French acétylène, coined by French chemist Marcellin Berthelot, from acetyl, from Latin acētum (“vinegar”) (from aceō (“to be sour”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”)) + Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “substance”) (from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“juice, liquid”)).
Borrowed from French actionner, from Latin actionāre.

parole.significato: to do something; to act; to function; to perform
parole.testo: Borrowed from French agir, itself from Latin agere.
Borrowed from French alléger, from Latin alleviāre. Doublet of aliviar.
Borrowed from French ambulance, from Latin ambulantia. By surface analysis, ambular + -ância.

parole.significato: ammonite (any of an extinct group of cephalopods of the subfamily Ammonoidea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ammonite, from Latin Ammōnis cornū (literally “horn of Ammon”), named by Pliny the Elder.
From French anis, from Old French anis, from Latin anīsum, from Ancient Greek ἂνισον (ànison).
Borrowed from French anormal, from Latin anōrmālis. By surface analysis, a- + normal.
Borrowed from French appétit, from Latin appetītus.
Borrowed from French harpon, from Latin harpago, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”).
Unadapted borrowing from French auteur. Doublet of autor.
Borrowed from French avion (“airplane”), coined by Clément Ader after Latin avis (“bird”), equivalent to ave + -ão.
Borrowed from French betterave; ultimately from Latin bēta (“beet”) + rapa (“turnip”).
Borrowed from French béton (“concrete”), from Latin bitūmen (“asphalt”), from Gaulish *bitu. Doublet of betume.
Borrowed from French biberon (“baby bottle”), ultimately from Latin bibere (“to drink”).
Borrowed from French billet, from Old French billette, from Latin bulla.
Borrowed from French bolide.

From French carabine (“carbine”), from carabin (“dragoon”), from regional escarrabin (“grave digger”), from Middle French scarabée, from Latin scarabaeus (“beetle”), from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”).

parole.significato: to sign, to stamp, to seal (a document)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chanceler, from Latin cancellāre. Doublet of cancelar.

parole.significato: charm (quality of inspiring delight or admiration)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French charme, from Latin carmen (“song, recitement, incantation”).

parole.significato: an agricultural instrument similar to a plough
parole.testo: From French charrue, from Latin carrūca (“Gaulish cart”).
Borrowed from French cistre, from Middle French citre, from Latin cithara. Doublet of cítara, guitarra, and cítola.
From French climatérique, from Latin clīmactēricus, from Ancient Greek κλιμακτηρικός (klimaktērikós), from κλῑμᾰκτήρ (klīmăktḗr) + -ικός (-ikós), from κλῖμαξ (klîmax).
From French coïncider, from Latin coincidere. By surface analysis, co- + incidir.

parole.significato: to command; to order (to give a direct order)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French commander, from Latin commandāre, variant of commendāre. Doublet of encomendar.
Borrowed from French combustible, from Latin combustus (“burning”).

parole.significato: compress (cloth used to dress or apply pressure to wounds)
parole.testo: From French compresse, from Latin compressus, past participle of comprimĕre.

parole.significato: conduit (duct or tube into which electrical cables may be pulled)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French conduite, from Latin conducta. Doublet of conduta.
Borrowed from French coryphée, from Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader of the chorus in an Ancient Greek drama”). Spelling influenced by Etymology 1.

parole.significato: harpsichord (keyboard instrument which produces sound by plucking the strings)
parole.testo: From French clavier (“keyboard”), from Latin clāvis (“key”).

parole.significato: crepe; crêpe (light fabric with a crinkled surface)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French crêpe, from Latin crispus. Doublet of crespo.
Borrowed from French crétin (“fool”), from Alpine French crestin (“Christian”), from Latin Chrīstiānus. Doublet of cristão, Cristiano, and Cristian.
Borrowed from French crime, from Latin crīmen.

parole.significato: croissant (a flaky roll or pastry in a form of a crescent)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French croissant, present participle of verb croître (“to grow”). Doublet of crescente.

parole.significato: cubism (an artistic movement characterized by the depiction of natural forms as geometric structures of planes)
parole.testo: From French cubisme, from Latin cubus (“mass, quantity”), from Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos, “cube, square”).
Borrowed from French dame, from Latin domina. Doublet of dona.
From French dentifrice, from Latin dentifricium.
Borrowed from French diabolo, coined based on Latin diabolus (“devil”). Doublet of diabo and diabre.
Borrowed from French diatribe.
From French duplicata, from Latin duplicāta (littera), from duplicātus. Doublet of duplicada.

parole.significato: to edit (to change a text or document)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French éditer (“to edit”), from Latin ēditus, perfect passive participle of ēdō (“to bring forth; bring about”).

parole.parola: entre o cão e o lobo
parole.significato: between a dog and a wolf
parole.testo: From French entre chien et loup (“between a dog and a wolf”), from Latin inter canem et lupum (“id.”).
From French store, from Latin storea. Doublet of esteira.
Borrowed from French eugenie, from Latin eugenīa, Ancient Greek εὐγενής (eugenḗs).
Borrowed from French évoluer, from Latin ēvolvere. Doublet of evolver.
From French explosif, ultimately from Latin explōsus, remodelled with the cognate suffix -ivo.

parole.significato: extrusion (process where a billet of material is pushed through a die)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French extrusion, from Latin extrūdere (“to extrude”).
From French festival, ultimately from Latin fēstīvālis.

parole.significato: fillet (strip of deboned meat or fish)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French filet, ultimately from Latin fīlum (“thread”). Doublet of filete.

parole.significato: only used in a for de
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from French for. Alternatively, an apocopic form of foro.

parole.significato: forge (workshop in which metals are shaped)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French forge, itself from Latin fabrica. Doublet of frágua and fábrica.

parole.significato: frenzy (state of wild activity or panic)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French frénésie, from Old French frenesie, from Latin phrenesis, from Ancient Greek *φρένησις (*phrénēsis), a later equivalent of φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”).
Borrowed from French fonctionner (“to function; to work”), from fonction + -er, from Latin fūnctiōnem (“function”). By surface analysis, função + -ar.
Borrowed from French grue, from Latin grūs.
Borrowed from French hydraulique.
Borrowed from French hiéroglyphique. By surface analysis, hieróglifo + -ico.
Borrowed from French hôtel, from Latin hospitāle. Doublet of hospital and hospedal.
From French jable (“croze”), from Latin gabulum (“gallows”).
Borrowed from French journal, from Latin diurnālis, from diēs (“day”). Doublet of diurno.

parole.significato: lymphatic (pertaining to lymph or lymphatic system)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lymphatique, from Latin lymphāticus. By surface analysis, linfa + -ático.
Borrowed from French maman, from Latin mamma.
Borrowed from French maison, from Latin mānsiōnem. Cognate with English mansion.
From French mètre, from Latin metrum, from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure”).

parole.significato: fashion (current (constantly changing) trend, favored for frivolous rather than practical, logical, or intellectual rea…
parole.testo: From French mode (“fashion; trend”), from Latin modus (“measure; manner, method”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”).
Borrowed from French moteur, from Latin mōtōrem.
Borrowed from French niche, from Old French niche, from nichier (“make a nest”), from Latin nīdus (“nest”).

parole.significato: wafer (disk of flour used to seal letters)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French oublée, from Latin oblata.
Borrowed from French ogre, from Latin Orcus (“god of the underworld”), from Ancient Greek Ὅρκος (Hórkos).
Borrowed from French paralysie, from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”).
Unadapted borrowing from French parkour, a respelling of parcours (“course, route”), from Latin percursus. Doublet of percurso.
Borrowed from French pavillon, Old French paveillon, from Latin pāpiliōnem.
From French pistache, from Latin pistacium, from Ancient Greek πιστάκιον (pistákion).

From French pneumatique, from Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breathe”).
Borrowed from French positivisme (“positivism”), from positif (“positive”), from Latin posītīvus (“positive”), from the past participle stem of pōnō (“to place”).
Borrowed from French positiviste (“positivist”), from positif (“positive”), from Latin posītīvus (“positive”), from the past participle stem of pōnō (“to place”).

parole.significato: premier (title of the head of government of certain countries)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French premier. Doublet of primeiro and primário.
From French prisonnier (“prisoner”), from prison (“prison”), from Old French prison, from Latin prehēnsiō (“seizing”), from prehendō (“to seize”).

parole.significato: reaction (action in response to an event)
parole.testo: From French réaction, from Latin reactiōnem, from the verb reago, from re- (“again”) + ago (“to act”).
Borrowed from French responsable, from Latin respōnsus, from respondere.

parole.significato: restaurant (an eating establishment in which diners are served food at their tables)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French restaurant.
Borrowed from French rétro, ultimately from Latin retrō. Doublet of redor.
Borrowed from French rétro, ultimately from Latin retrō. Doublet of redor.
From French roulé.
Borrowed from French sanitaire, a learned formation created from the base of Latin sānitās (cf. sanidade).

parole.significato: Zionism (movement seeking a Jewish homeland in Israel)
parole.testo: From Sião + -ismo, on the model of French sionisme, from Latin Sīōn.

parole.significato: siren (device that produces a piercing loud sounds as an alarm of signal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sirène, from Latin sirēna. Doublet of sereia and sirena.
From French soporifique, from Latin sopor (“deep sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swepōr, from *swep-.
Unadapted borrowing from French souvenir.
From French sudorifique, from Latin sūdor (“sweat”) + -ificus (“bringing, making”).

parole.significato: soufflé (baked dish made from beaten egg whites)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French soufflé, from souffler (“to puff”), from Latin sufflāre (“to blow, to puff up, to inflate”).
From suicida + -ar, on the model of French suicider, ultimately from Latin sui + caedere.
Borrowed from French surprise, from Old French surprendre (“to overtake”), from sur- (“over”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin prendere (“to seize”).
Borrowed from French souvenir.
Borrowed from French thrène, from Latin thrēnus, from Ancient Greek θρῆνος (thrênos).

parole.significato: turbine (rotary machines that use the energy of a stream of fluid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French turbine (“turbine”), itself borrowed from Latin turbinem (“circular movement, top, reel, spindle”). Compare trovão, an inherited doublet through a Vulgar Latin variant.
From French technique, from Latin technicus, from Ancient Greek τεχνικός (tekhnikós), from τέχνη (tékhnē, “art, skill, trade”).

parole.significato: plant (factory or industrial facility), especially a large one
parole.testo: Borrowed from French usine (“factory; works”), from Latin officīna. Doublet of oficina.
From French viser, from Latin vīsere.
